Translate in the Greek order, "In whom (not as Alford, 'in which') mystery; Christ is Himself the 'mystery' (<reference osisRef="Col.2.2">Col 2:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.16">1Ti 3:16</reference>), and to Christ the relative refers) are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden." The "all" here, answers to "all" in <reference osisRef="Col.2.2">Col 2:2</reference>; as "treasures" answer to the "riches"; it is from the treasures that the riches (<reference osisRef="Col.2.2">Col 2:2</reference>) are derived. "Are" is the predicate of the sentence; all the treasures ARE in Him; hidden is predicated of the state or manner in which they are in Him. Like a mine of unknown and inexhaustible wealth, the treasures of wisdom are all in Him hidden, but not in order to remain so; they only need to be explored for you to attain "unto the riches" in them (<reference osisRef="Col.2.2">Col 2:2</reference>); but until you, Colossians, press after attaining the full knowledge (see on <reference osisRef="Col.2.2">Col 2:2</reference>) of them, they remain "hidden." Compare the parable, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.44">Mt 13:44</reference>, "treasure hid." This sense suits the scope of the apostle, and sets aside Alford's objection that "the treasures are not hidden, but revealed." "Hidden" plainly answers to "mystery" (<reference osisRef="Col.2.2">Col 2:2</reference>), which is designed by God, if we be faithful to our privileges, not to remain hidden, but to be revealed (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.7">1Co 2:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.8">8</reference>). Still as the mine is unfathomable, there will, through eternity, be always fresh treasures in Him to be drawn forth from their hidden state.<div eID="gen36351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36352" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wisdom--</hi>general, and as to experimental and practical truth; whence comes "understanding" (<reference osisRef="Col.2.2">Col 2:2</reference>).<div eID="gen36352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36353" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">knowledge--</hi>special and intellectual, in regard to doctrinal truth; whence comes "the full knowledge" (<reference osisRef="Col.2.2">Col 2:2</reference>). <div eID="gen36353" type="x-p"/>

Rooted--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Eph.3.17">Ep 3:17</reference>).<div eID="gen36361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36362" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">built up--</hi>Greek, "being builded up." As "rooted" implies their vitality; so "builded up," massive solidity. As in the Song of Solomon, when one image is not sufficient to express the varied aspects of divine truth, another is employed to supply the idea required. Translate, "Having been buried with Him in your baptism." The past participle is here coincident in time with the preceding verb, "ye were (Greek) circumcised." Baptism is regarded as the burial of the old carnal life, to which the act of immersion symbolically corresponds; and in warm climates where immersion is safe, it is the mode most accordant with the significance of the ordinance; but the spirit of the ordinance is kept by affusion, where immersion would be inconvenient or dangerous; to insist on literal immersion in all cases would be mere legal ceremonialism (<reference osisRef="Rom.6.3">Ro 6:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.6.4">4</reference>).<div eID="gen36381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36382" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">are risen--</hi>rather as Greek, "were raised with Him."<div eID="gen36382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36383" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">through the faith, &c.--</hi>by means of your faith in the operation of God; so "faith of," for "faith in" (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.12">Ep 3:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.3.9">Php 3:9</reference>). Faith in God's mighty operation in raising again Jesus, is saving faith (<reference osisRef="Rom.4.24">Ro 4:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.10.9">10:9</reference>); and it is wrought in the soul by His same "mighty working" whereby He "raised Jesus from the dead" (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.19">Ep 1:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.20">20</reference>). Bengel seems to me (not as Alford understands him) to express the latter sense, namely, "Through the faith which is a work of the operation of God who," &c. <reference osisRef="Eph.1.19">Ep 1:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.20">20</reference> accords with this; the same mighty power of God is exercised in raising one spiritually dead to the life of faith, as was "wrought in Christ when God raised Him literally from the dead." However, "faith of" usually is "faith in" (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.22">Ro 3:22</reference>); but there is no grammatical impropriety in understanding it "the faith which is the effect of the operation of God" (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.8">Ep 2:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.13">1Th 2:13</reference>). As His literal resurrection is the ground of the power put forth in our spiritual resurrection now, so it is a pledge of our literal resurrection hereafter (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.11">Ro 8:11</reference>). <div eID="gen36383" type="x-p"/>

Alford, Ellicott, and others translate the Greek to accord with the translation of the same Greek, <reference osisRef="Col.3.9">Col 3:9</reference>, "Stripping off from Himself the principalities and the powers: " God put off from Himself the angels, that is, their ministry, not employing them to be promulgators of the Gospel in the way that He had given the law by their "disposition" or ministry (<reference osisRef="Acts.7.53">Ac 7:53</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.3.19">Ga 3:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.2.2">He 2:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.5">5</reference>): God manifested Himself without a veil in Jesus. "The principalities and THE powers" refers back to <reference osisRef="Col.2.10">Col 2:10</reference>, Jesus, "the Head of all principality and power," and <reference osisRef="Col.1.16">Col 1:16</reference>. In the sacrifice of Jesus on the cross, God subjected all the principalities, &c., to Jesus, declaring them to be powerless as to His work and His people (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.21">Ep 1:21</reference>). Thus Paul's argument against those grafting on Christianity Jewish observances, along with angel-worship, is, whatever part angels may be supposed to have had under the law, now at an end, God having put the legal dispensation itself away. But the objection is, that the context seems to refer to a triumph over bad angels: in <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.14">2Co 2:14</reference>, however, Christ's triumph over those subjected to Him, is not a triumph for destruction, but for their salvation, so that good angels may be referred to (<reference osisRef="Col.1.20">Col 1:20</reference>). But the Greek middle is susceptible of English Version, "having spoiled," or, literally [Tittmann], "having completely stripped," or "despoiled" for Himself (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.8.38">Ro 8:38</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.24">1Co 15:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.6.2">Ep 6:2</reference>). English Version accords with <reference osisRef="Matt.12.29">Mt 12:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.11.22">Lu 11:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.2.14">He 2:14</reference>. Many of the Latins, "In Himself" or "in Him." <reference osisRef="Eph.2.16">Ep 2:16</reference> favors English Version, "reconcile ... by the cross, having slain the enmity thereby."
